passages.note: House third-reading passage vote; Soliday appears in the Yea column and the tally is 63-31, so the near-unanimous rule does not apply.

passages.provision_quote: A governmental entity may substantially burden a person's exercise of religion only if the governmental entity demonstrates that application of the burden to the person: (1) is in furtherance of a compelling governmental interest; and (2) is the least restrictive means of furthering that compelling governmental interest.

Bill-details page for the same record group; it carries only the digest and the author and sponsor lists, and Soliday is in neither, so it shows no act of his and is not relied on.

rows.reasoning: Soliday voted Yea on House third-reading passage of SB 101 (2015), a single-subject religious freedom restoration bill (Roll Call 305, "Yea 63 Nay 31 Excused 5 Not Voting 0"), whose enrolled text bars a governmental entity from substantially burdening a person's exercise of religion "even if the burden results from a rule of general applicability" absent a compelling interest pursued by the least restrictive means, and lets the burdened person assert the chapter "as a claim or defense in a judicial or administrative proceeding". That operative content is the rung that would "protect religious freedom and allow faith-based exemptions from laws that conflict with sincere religious beliefs", with the exemption keyed to "any exercise of religion, whether or not compelled by, or central to, a system of religious belief". The rung granting religious organizations "complete autonomy in their operations and hiring practices" is excluded by the bill's own compelling-interest test and by its bar on claims against private employers, and no rung clause about equal treatment or anti-discrimination protections appears in the text, which exempts no statute or ordinance "unless a state statute expressly exempts" it.
